 How Many 2028 Presidential Campaigns Will Launch in 2026? 
 By Dr. Eric Ostermeier | November 15, 2026 | 1 
 Tweet 
 Share 
 Less than six percent of presidential candidates announced their campaigns during the year of the preceding midterm or earlier 
 With the midterm elections in the rear-view mirror, attention will soon turn to the presidential election cycle – with expectations that an open seat race will draw many candidates from both major parties.
 Thus far, no non-fringe candidate has filed for the presidency in 2028. Who will be the first out of the gate and when will such an announcement be made?
 During the 2024 presidential election cycle, two candidates announced their candidacies as early as the year of the midterm: former Montana Secretary of State Corey Stapleton on November 11, 2022 and former President Donald Trump four days later on November 15th.
 The remaining 15 GOP and Democratic candidates all declared their candidacies for the office in 2023.
 During the modern primary era (1972-), only 13 of the 223 major party candidacies by non-fringe candidates were launched during the year of the midterm (or earlier):
 1976 cycle: Arizona Democratic U.S. Representative Mo Udall (November 23, 1974; 710 days out from Election Day)
 1976 cycle: Former Georgia Democratic Governor Jimmy Carter (December 12, 1974; 691 days)
 1980 cycle: Illinois GOP U.S. Representative Phil Crane (August 2, 1978; 825 days)
 1988 cycle: Former Delaware Republican Governor Pete du Pont IV (September 16, 1986; 784 days)
 2008 cycle: Former Alaska Democratic U.S. Senator Mike Gravel (April 17, 2006; 932 days)
 2008 cycle: Iowa Democratic Governor Tom Vilsack (November 30, 2006; 705 days)
 2008 cycle: Ohio Democratic U.S. Representative Dennis Kucinich (December 11, 2006; 694 days)
 2008 cycle: Former North Carolina U.S. Senator John Edwards (December 28, 2006; 677 days)
 2020 cycle: Maryland Democratic U.S. Representative John Delaney (pictured) (July 28, 2017; a record 1,194 days)
 2020 cycle: New York Democratic entrepreneur Andrew Yang (November 6, 2017; 1,093 days)
 2020 cycle: West Virginia Democratic State Senator Richard Ojeda (November 11, 2018; 723 days)
 2024 cycle: Former Montana Secretary of State Corey Stapleton (November 11, 2022; 725 days)
 2024 cycle: Former President Donald Trump (November 15, 2022; 721 days)
 Only two of these candidates were nominated – Carter and Trump – and both were subsequently elected.
 Of the remaining 11 candidacies, only Udall carried any states during the primaries (the caucuses of his home state Arizona) – eventually placing second behind Carter in the 1976 Democratic total delegate count.
 Just three of the 10 other candidates received even a handful of delegates (Crane, du Pont, and Edwards).
 The average announcement date for major party presidential campaigns since 1972 has been 523 days out from Election Day – or June 3, 2027.

 1 Comment 
 Flickertail-Pembina on November 15, 2026 at 7:35 pm 
 Ex-SoS Stapleton also ended up leaving the nomination derby before the first-in-the-nation Iowa precinct caucuses. For the 2024 cycle, Stapleton, Doug Burgum, and Larry Elder were the only Republican candidates from both outside the South and west of the River Mississippi.
 There seems to be a lack of consensus with regard to the real start of a presidential election cycle. Some media outlets (perhaps in order to lure in more viewers) declare the day after “election day” (midterm) as such. Others stick to the traditional two-year period as comprising the cycle.
 VP Bowman/Hamel/Vance seems certain to become a ’28 candidate should he end up *ascending* to the office. Absent that, he is apt to wait until well after the “average announcement date” for his announcement – if he is seeking the office at all, that is.
 “… or 3 of June 2027” What is the likelihood that ex-Vice President (and candidate for both the 2024 and 2020 cycles) Kamala Harris will make an announcement – of *either candidacy or non-candidacy* – at any time during the second quarter?
